en.html:
...Nahin aayi. Ritsu did not come back.

Not home. Not to school. Not to us.

Now people were getting alarmed. Disappearances were nothing unusual in Kanto these days. Achchha, so? Somebody you knew disappears, and you are supposed to relax because it is a popular occurrence?

Suzukawa came to our classroom only that morning. Afterward, apparently, his rounds were Ritsu's house, the staff room, the police station. Several times I saw him striding down a corridor or across the schoolyard, his face stern.

They must have filed a missing-person report. But surely neither sir nor the family expected that to settle anything. A coin in the shrine box. Bhagwan, if you are listening, please.

Even a show of investigation would be better than usual. More likely some fellow would put one careless entry in a register. Bas, likh diya. Ritsu missing, paperwork present.

In the past few years, not one story had reached me of the police protecting citizens. Big case, small case, kuch nahin. When Rokuhara needed anti-Shogunate people rounded up, apparently it worked them like subcontractors. That much they could do.

Rely on them? Not even this much.

We would have to do it ourselves.

I muttered over the map of Kamakura in my head. Tadayasu said nothing. Probably he agreed. With him you had to allow a little time before declaring an idea intelligent; sometimes he was only waiting for you to finish being wrong.

We had started with Ritsu's movements after she parted from him two nights ago. She roamed widely, haan, but this was her home ground. And Ritsu moving through a place without anybody noticing—arre, that would take preparation.

Put in enough legwork, and even two amateurs playing detective might manage something. We actually had a few results already. No brilliant deduction required. Just keep walking until the town surrendered one useful answer.

Konatsu was checking Ritsu's friends separately. Mostly girls. Boys attached to that expedition would only be extra luggage. For once we had improved a conversation before it began, by not being in it.

We reached the station.

The railway was Kanto's main transport artery. An ordinary citizen making regular use of this artery? Bhai, the blood could travel. You could not. Once, things had been different.

Now it was practically the Shogunate's service train. Soldiers and military supplies, that was what it carried. Civilians were allowed, haan. First produce a fare so unreasonable that the permission became a joke.

For Edo or Sunpu, better take a boat. Slower, but cheap, with dependable sailings.

So Ritsu taking a train from Kamakura and going somewhere was hardly likely. We hadn't come here thinking that, anyway.

Only then did I notice.

Not her. Arre, the music. I had been hearing her play all this time. My ears had received it perfectly well and apparently decided the rest of me had no need to know.

A large stringed instrument. She held it like a lover—or perhaps a child—and drew her bow across it.

Such weight in the sound. Full, but quiet. I thought of wind drifting deep inside a forest, where sunlight could not reach.

Nobody's skin to touch. Nobody's ears to enter.

Not one person stopped before her. The crowd kept hurrying past.

Later, perhaps, a melody would cross their minds. Kahan suna tha? Where had they heard it? They wouldn't even remember having heard it at all. The brain would bring home something lovely and lose the address, then expect congratulations for the discovery.

Now that I was actually listening—

Beautiful. Her playing was beautiful.
